title: Indexing
subtitle: Internal mechanics of B+ Trees, LSM-Trees, composite index prefix rules, selectivity, and covering indexes.
keyTakeaways: B+ Trees optimize for read latency and range scans via balanced leaf nodes on disk; LSM-Trees optimize for write throughput via sequential append-only flushes.

Composite indexes enforce the Leftmost Prefix Rule: an index on `(status, created_at)` accelerates queries filtering by `status` or `(status, created_at)`, but is useless for queries filtering by `created_at` alone.
Covering indexes include all queried columns in the index structure itself, allowing the database to execute Index-Only Scans without reading the heap table.
architectureDiagram:
B+ TREE STORAGE ENGINE VS LSM-TREE STORAGE ENGINE
B+ TREE (PostgreSQL / InnoDB): Balanced Tree on Disk
[ Root Node ] -> [ Internal Nodes ] -> [ Leaf Pages (Linked List) ]
- Reads: O(log N) fast page lookups; ideal for range scans
- Writes: In-place page updates; random disk I/O and page splits

LSM-TREE (Cassandra / RocksDB): Log-Structured Merge-Tree
[ In-Memory Memtable ] -> Flushed to -> [ Immutable SSTables on Disk ]
- Writes: Sequential disk appends (Fast!)
- Compaction: Background compaction merges SSTables, consuming disk IOPS

sections.heading: B+ Trees vs LSM-Trees Under the Hood
sections.body: Database indexing is dictated by underlying storage engine mechanics. Relational databases like Postgres and MySQL use B+ Trees. In a B+ Tree, data records or heap pointers are stored exclusively in sorted leaf nodes linked as a doubly linked list, with internal nodes holding navigation keys. This guarantees predictable `O(log N)` read and range-scan performance, but random updates force in-place disk modifications and page splits. LSM-Trees (used in Cassandra, RocksDB, and ScyllaDB) buffer writes in an in-memory memtable (Red-Black tree) and append flushed data to immutable sorted string tables (SSTables) on disk, achieving massive write throughput by converting random writes into sequential I/O.
bullets: B+ Tree Leaf Pointers: Leaf pages contain pointers to the actual table heap rows, unless the index is clustered (like MySQL InnoDB's primary key).

LSM Compaction Overhead: In LSM engines, reads must check the memtable, bloom filters, and multiple SSTables. Periodic background compaction merges SSTables to reclaim deleted tombstone space, consuming significant background disk IOPS.
Write Amplification: Every B+ Tree index added to a table increases the disk write amplification of every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`.

codeSnippet.title: Composite Index and Covering Index Definition in PostgreSQL
codeSnippet.code:
-- 1. Composite Index: Supports (tenant_id), and (tenant_id, created_at)
-- Does NOT accelerate queries filtering by 'created_at' alone!
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_tenant_date 
ON orders (tenant_id, created_at DESC);

-- 2. Covering Index (Index-Only Scan):
-- Stores 'total_amount' directly in the leaf pages via INCLUDE clause.
-- The database reads the result directly from the index without touching table heap!
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_covering 
ON orders (tenant_id, status) 
INCLUDE (total_amount, user_id);

sections.heading: Selectivity, Cardinality, and the Leftmost Prefix Rule
sections.body: Creating an index does not guarantee the database query planner will use it. The planner evaluates column cardinality (the number of distinct values) and selectivity (the percentage of table rows matching the filter). If a query matches 30% of the table rows, the query planner will ignore the index and execute a full sequential scan because random page seeks across the index cost more than a linear sequential disk read.
bullets: High vs Low Cardinality: Primary keys, UUIDs, and email addresses have high cardinality (ideal for indexes); boolean flags (`is_active`) have low cardinality (indexes are ignored unless combined in composite keys).
Partial Indexes: In Postgres, index only the relevant subset (`CREATE INDEX ... WHERE status = 'PENDING'`). This keeps index size small and avoids indexing millions of archived records.
Index-Only Scans: When all columns referenced in the `SELECT`, `WHERE`, and `ORDER BY` clauses reside in the index itself, the database avoids reading the underlying table data pages completely.

tradeOffs.pros: Fast point reads and range scans; deterministic lookup times; immediate space reclamation on deletes.
tradeOffs.cons: Random write patterns reduce insertion throughput; index fragmentation requires periodic rebuilding.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Read-heavy relational workloads, transactional databases, and ordered range pagination.

tradeOffs.pros: Near line-rate sequential write performance; superior storage compression ratios on disk.
tradeOffs.cons: Slower read latency (read amplification); background compaction can cause sudden disk I/O and latency spikes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Write-heavy ingestion, IoT time-series telemetry, logging systems, and event ledgers.

interviewTip: Demonstrate database mastery by explaining composite index ordering: 'When creating a composite index on `(status, created_at)`, equality filter columns must come first, followed by range filter columns. The database can seek to the equality value and then perform a sequential range scan along the index leaf pages.'
